title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
authors: William Fedus, Barret Zoph, Noam Shazeer

pages.title: Scale by adding experts, not by making each token do more work

blocks.html: The wall this paper hits. A dense Transformer scales by making every parameter participate in every forward pass. Double the parameters and you double the floating-point operations (FLOPs) spent on each token. Quality keeps improving with size, but the compute bill grows in lockstep — that coupling is the wall.

The key move: decouple parameters from compute. A Mixture of Experts (MoE) layer holds many parallel copies of the feed-forward network (the ‘experts’) but routes each token to only a small subset of them. The model can carry, say, 10× or 100× the parameters of a dense baseline while spending roughly the same FLOPs per token, because each token only ever touches a handful of experts. Parameters become cheap; compute stays fixed.

What Switch simplifies. Prior MoE work (Shazeer et al., 2017) routed each token to its top-2 experts, on the belief that you need at least two so the router gets a useful comparison gradient. Switch Transformer routes each token to exactly one expert (top-1). This ‘switch’ routing is simpler, cuts the router compute and the communication cost roughly in half, and — surprisingly — works at least as well.

We design models with up to 1.6 trillion parameters and demonstrate they can be trained stably. The Switch Transformer achieves a 4-7x speedup over a strongly tuned T5-Base, and a 4x speedup over T5-Large, at the same computational cost. We further show that large sparse models trained with low precision (bfloat16) reach quality comparable to high precision dense models.

Where it sits. Switch is built on Google's T5 (Raffel et al., 2019) and trained on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus (C4). It descends from Shazeer's 2017 MoE-LSTM work and GShard, and its top-1-plus-capacity recipe became the template for the modern MoE models (GLaM, Mixtral, DeepSeek-MoE) that dominate the trillion-parameter frontier today.

pages.title: Replacing the FFN with a Switch FFN

blocks.html: What gets changed. Take a standard Transformer block. Inside it sits a feed-forward network (FFN) that every token passes through identically. The Switch Transformer keeps the rest of the block (self-attention, layer norm, residuals) untouched and replaces just that single FFN with a Switch layer: $N$ independent FFNs — the experts — plus a small router that decides which one expert each token visits (Figure 2).

A worked example. Suppose $N = 4$ experts and the word ‘More’ arrives with hidden state $x$. The router scores all four experts, say [0.5, 0.1, 0.3, 0.1] after softmax. Top-1 routing sends ‘More’ only to expert 1 (score 0.5); experts 2, 3, 4 do nothing for this token. The next word ‘Parameters’ might route to expert 3. Different tokens take different paths through the same layer — that is the whole idea.

The router. For a token's hidden state $x \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$, a learned matrix $W_r$ produces logits $h(x) = W_r \cdot x$, one per expert. A softmax turns them into a probability over the $N$ experts:

Reading it term by term. $h(x)_i$ is the router's raw score (logit) for expert $i$; $e^{h(x)_i}$ exponentiates it; the denominator $\sum_{j=1}^{N} e^{h(x)_j}$ sums the exponentials over all $N$ experts so the result normalizes to 1. So $p_i(x)$ is the probability the router assigns to expert $i$. $W_r \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$ is the only new parameter the router adds.
The Switch output. Let $i^*$ be the highest-scoring expert. The token is sent there, and the expert's output is scaled by that router probability:

Why multiply by $p_{i^*}(x)$. $\text{Expert}_{i^*}(x)$ is the chosen FFN's output. The scalar $p_{i^*}(x)$ is what makes the router trainable: the $\arg\max$ itself is non-differentiable, but multiplying the output by the router probability means gradients flow back into $W_r$ — if the expert's output reduced the loss, the router learns to assign it a higher probability next time. All other experts contribute nothing for this token, so only one FFN's worth of compute is spent.

Design rationale for top-1. The 2017 intuition was that you need $k \geq 2$ experts to give the router a comparison signal. Switch shows top-1 is enough: it halves the router computation and the cross-device communication, lowers the memory for expert buffers, and in practice trains just as well. Less machinery, same result — the recurring theme of the paper.

pages.title: Load balancing — keeping the experts busy

blocks.html: The failure mode. Routing is learned, and learned routers have a nasty tendency to collapse: early in training one or two experts get slightly better, the router sends them more tokens, they improve faster, and a feedback loop concentrates almost all traffic on a few experts. The rest sit idle. That wastes the whole point of having many experts and creates a compute bottleneck on the hot ones.

A concrete picture. With $N = 128$ experts and a balanced batch, each expert should see about $1/128 \approx 0.8\%$ of tokens. A collapsed router might send 40% of tokens to expert 5 and 0% to dozens of others. The auxiliary loss below is what prevents that.
The differentiable load-balancing loss. For each batch $\mathcal{B}$ of $T$ tokens routed across $N$ experts, an auxiliary term is added to the training loss:

Reading it term by term. $f_i$ is the fraction of tokens actually dispatched to expert $i$ — the indicator $\mathbb{1}\{\cdot\}$ counts a token when expert $i$ was its top choice, and dividing by $T$ makes it a fraction. $P_i$ is the average router probability assigned to expert $i$ across the batch. $\alpha$ is a small weight (the paper uses $\alpha = 10^{-2}$) controlling how hard balance is enforced; $N$ rescales so the loss is order-1 regardless of expert count.

Why this exact product. $f_i$ alone is non-differentiable (it depends on the hard $\arg\max$), so you cannot backprop through it — but $P_i$ is smooth, and using $f_i$ as a fixed weight on $P_i$ gives a differentiable surrogate. The sum $\sum_i f_i P_i$ is minimized when both $f_i$ and $P_i$ equal $1/N$ for every expert, i.e. perfectly uniform routing. So minimizing $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$ gently pushes traffic toward an even spread without dictating which token goes where.

Trivia / lineage. This is a simplification of the more elaborate balancing losses in Shazeer et al. (2017) and GShard (Lepikhin et al., 2020). Variants of exactly this $f_i \cdot P_i$ auxiliary loss are still used in modern MoE training; getting balance right remains one of the central engineering challenges of sparse models.

The hardware problem. On a TPU/GPU, tensor shapes must be fixed and known ahead of time — you cannot have an expert whose buffer grows or shrinks depending on how many tokens happen to route to it this batch. So each expert is given a fixed number of slots, the expert capacity, and the system must decide what to do when more tokens want an expert than it has slots.
The capacity formula. Capacity is set by a tunable capacity factor:

Reading it term by term. tokens per batch / N is the number of tokens each expert would get under perfectly uniform routing. The capacity factor (e.g. 1.0, 1.25, 2.0) is slack: at 1.0 each expert has exactly its fair share of slots; at 1.25 it has 25% headroom to absorb routing imbalance. The ceiling $\lceil \cdot \rceil$ rounds up to a whole number of slots.

Overflow = dropped tokens. If routing sends more tokens to an expert than it has slots (Figure 3, right), the excess tokens overflow: they skip the FFN entirely and pass through unchanged via the residual connection. They are not an error — the residual still carries their representation to the next layer — they just miss this expert's transformation.

The trade-off. A higher capacity factor means fewer dropped tokens (better quality) but more wasted compute and memory on empty slots (lower efficiency). Switch shows the model trains successfully even with a mild drop rate — typically under 1% of tokens dropped with capacity factor around 1.25 — because the load-balancing loss keeps imbalance small. The paper sweeps capacity factors 1.0–2.0 and finds the sweet spot around 1.25.

Why this matters. Capacity factor is the single knob that trades quality against efficiency in a sparse model, and getting to use a low one (close to 1.0) is part of what makes Switch faster than top-2 MoE: fewer slots to fill, less data to shuffle between devices.

The stability problem. Sparse models with a hard $\arg\max$ router are notoriously twitchy to train — the routing decisions can swing wildly early on, and naive low-precision arithmetic makes it worse. This section is the engineering that makes trillion-parameter training actually converge rather than diverge.

Selective precision (the bfloat16 trick). Training in bfloat16 (16-bit brain floating point) halves memory and speeds up matmuls, but the router's softmax involves exponentials that are unstable in low precision. Switch's fix: cast the router's input to float32 just for the routing computation, then cast back. You get bfloat16 speed everywhere else and float32 stability exactly where it is needed — in the router.
By using selective precision only in the router, we obtain the speed and memory benefits of bfloat16 while matching the training stability of a full float32 model.

Smaller initialization. Switch shrinks the weight-initialization scale by a factor of 10 (drawing from a truncated normal with reduced variance). Smaller initial weights tame the early routing swings; the paper shows this alone improves both average quality (neg-log-perplexity from $-1.755$ to $-1.740$) and, more importantly, the variance across runs (std drops from $0.069$ to $0.008$) — making training far more reliable, not just better on average.

Expert dropout. When fine-tuning a giant sparse model on a small downstream task, it overfits easily. Switch applies a higher dropout rate inside the experts than elsewhere — e.g. 0.1 dropout on the dense layers but 0.4 on the expert layers. On the fine-tuning suite this lifts GLUE, CNNDM, SQuAD and SuperGLUE scores together (Table 4), recovering most of the gap to the dense baseline.

Why these three matter together. Selective precision buys speed without instability; small init buys low-variance convergence; expert dropout buys clean fine-tuning. None is glamorous, but each removes a specific failure mode that had previously made large sparse models a research curiosity rather than a practical tool.

pages.title: Speed and quality vs. T5 baselines

blocks.html: The headline comparison (Table 1). Holding the per-token FLOPs fixed (so the comparison is fair on compute), Switch-Base is dramatically faster to reach a target quality than the dense T5 it is built from. On a step basis and a wall-clock basis, the sparse model wins decisively.

The 7× figure (Figure 5). Trained on 32 TPUv3 cores against an equal-FLOP T5-Base, Switch-Base reaches the same pre-training quality threshold about 7× faster in wall-clock time. Against T5-Large the speedup is about 4×. The paper summarizes the range as a 4–7× speedup depending on the baseline and capacity factor — the number quoted in the abstract.

Scaling on a step basis (Figure 4). Increasing the number of experts — 2, 4, 8, …, up to 256 — at fixed FLOPs steadily lowers loss. More experts means more parameters but the same per-token compute, and the negative-log-perplexity keeps improving, demonstrating a clean ‘more sparse parameters help’ trend that is the engine of the whole approach.

Why this is the central result. It separates the two things people usually conflate: parameters and compute. Switch shows you can pour parameters in (via experts) and convert them into quality without paying the usual FLOP tax — the exact decoupling promised in the abstract, now measured.

Does the pre-training win transfer? A faster pre-training loss is only useful if it shows up on real tasks after fine-tuning. Switch fine-tunes its sparse models on the standard suite — SuperGLUE, GLUE, SQuAD, CNN/DailyMail summarization, the ARC and closed-book QA sets, Winogrande — and the gains carry over.

Distillation back to dense (Tables 6–8). A trillion-parameter sparse model is awkward to deploy. So Switch distills a sparse teacher into a small dense student: the student keeps about 30% of the quality gain the sparse model had over a dense baseline, while compressing the parameter count by up to ~95% (1.3B-parameter teacher down to a 223M dense student). You train sparse for speed, then ship dense for convenience.

Multilingual (Section 4.3). A multilingual Switch (mSwitch-Base) trained on 101 languages beats the dense mT5-Base on 91% of languages, with an average ~5× speedup to a fixed quality. Sparsity is not an English-only trick — the per-language capacity that experts provide is especially useful when the data is heterogeneous across languages.

The recurring lesson. Across pre-training, fine-tuning, distillation and multilingual settings, the same pattern holds: at equal compute, more sparse parameters help, and the resulting quality survives the trip to downstream tasks and even to a compressed dense deployment.

pages.title: Data, model, and expert parallelism — and Switch-C

blocks.html: The problem at trillion scale. 1.6 trillion parameters do not fit on one device, so the model must be split across many. Switch combines three kinds of parallelism (Figure 9): data parallelism (different cores see different batches), model parallelism (a single weight matrix is sharded across cores), and expert parallelism (different experts live on different cores). The genius of expert parallelism is that it adds parameters by adding cores, each holding its own experts, with no extra per-token compute.
The two flagship models (Table 9). Switch-XXL matches T5-XXL's per-token FLOPs (6.3T FLOPs/seq) but with 64 experts, reaching 395B parameters. Switch-C goes wide instead of deep:

Reading the table. Switch-C is the 1.6-trillion-parameter model — 1571B parameters spread over 2048 experts in 15 layers, with $d_{\text{model}} = 2080$ and 32 attention heads. It uses far less per-token compute than the much smaller dense T5-XXL (890B vs 6.3T FLOPs/seq) yet matches its perplexity. Switch-XXL, which is denser-per-expert, actually reaches the threshold faster per step than Switch-C — a hint that beyond some point adding raw experts has diminishing returns versus making each expert do more.

The honest caveats. The paper is candid that the largest models showed training instabilities, and that Switch-C, despite its enormous parameter count, was not the strongest per-FLOP performer — Switch-XXL's better compute-per-parameter ratio made it stronger on several downstream tasks. The trillion-parameter result is a feasibility demonstration as much as a recommendation.

Why 1.6T was the point. Before Switch, it was an open question whether MoE could be pushed to the trillion-parameter regime and stay trainable at all. Demonstrating that it could — on real hardware, with stable training — is what made sparsity a credible frontier-scaling strategy rather than a small-scale trick.

pages.title: MoE in the modern LLM stack

blocks.html: What Switch established. It was the cleanest demonstration that Mixture-of-Experts could scale to trillions of parameters and remain trainable. Its three simplifications — top-1 routing, a fixed expert capacity, and drop-on-overflow — plus the engineering (selective bfloat16 precision, small init, expert dropout) became the standard recipe everyone else copied.
We hope our work motivates sparse models as an effective architecture and that this encourages researchers and practitioners to consider these flexible models in natural language tasks, and beyond.

What it influenced. The modern MoE lineage runs directly through this paper: GLaM (Google's 1.2T MoE), GShard (its parallelism sibling), the open-weight Mixtral family from Mistral, DeepSeek-MoE, and the sparse architectures widely believed to power frontier models from OpenAI and others. MoE is now the dominant way to scale at the trillion-parameter frontier.

The big-picture takeaway. Switch reframed scaling: the question stopped being ‘how many FLOPs can we afford per token’ and became ‘how many parameters can we store and route to cheaply.’ That reframing — parameters are cheap, compute is the constraint — is one of the load-bearing ideas of the current era of large language models.

Connections in this collection. Switch sits on top of the original Transformer (Attention Is All You Need) and the T5 text-to-text framework, and its low-precision training story rhymes with quantization work like LLM.int8(). It is the sparsity counterpart to the dense-scaling story told by GPT-3.
